name: SQL
description: SQL is the language of relational databases: query, combine, change and design data stored in tables.

blocks.html:
Databases, Tables & SELECT

What is a database table?

A relational database stores information in tables. A table looks like a spreadsheet: every column has a name and a type (for example name is text and score is a whole number), and every row is one record, such as one student. SQL (Structured Query Language) is the language you use to ask the database questions and to change its data. The same basic SQL works in MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite, SQL Server and Oracle.

All the examples in this course use a small students table. Read it once, because you will see it in every lesson:

idnamecitydeptscore
1AyeshaLahoreCS85
2BilalKarachiSE72
3HiraLahoreCS91
4UsmanIslamabadEE64
5SaraKarachiSE78

Reading data with SELECT

SELECT is the command that reads data. You list the columns you want after SELECT and the table after FROM. A query always ends with a semicolon. SQL keywords are not case sensitive, but writing them in capital letters makes a query easier to read.

blocks.code:
SELECT name, city
FROM students;
blocks.output:
name   | city     
--------+-----------
 Ayesha | Lahore   
 Bilal  | Karachi  
 Hira   | Lahore   
 Usman  | Islamabad
 Sara   | Karachi  
(5 rows)

blocks.html:
The database returns a new table with only the two columns you asked for. The original table is not changed: SELECT never modifies data.

All columns, aliases and DISTINCT

A star * means "every column". It is handy while exploring, but in real projects list the columns you need, because it is faster and clearer. Use AS to give a column a friendlier name (an alias) in the result. Use DISTINCT to remove repeated values.

blocks.output:
city     
-----------
 Lahore   
 Karachi  
 Islamabad
(3 rows)

 student | marks
---------+-------
 Ayesha  | 85   
 Bilal   | 72   
 Hira    | 91   
 Usman   | 64   
 Sara    | 78   
(5 rows)

blocks.html:
Without DISTINCT the city list would show Lahore and Karachi twice. An alias only changes the heading in the result, not the table.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the comma between column names, or adding an extra comma before FROM.
  • Putting FROM before SELECT. The order is always SELECT then FROM.
  • Using double quotes for text. In standard SQL text values use single quotes, like 'Lahore'.

Key Points

  • A table has columns (name and type) and rows (records).
  • SELECT columns FROM table; reads data and never changes it.
  • * selects all columns; AS renames a column in the result.
  • DISTINCT removes duplicate values from the result.
  • Text values use single quotes.

Filtering & Sorting Rows

Filtering with WHERE

Most of the time you do not want every row. The WHERE clause keeps only the rows for which a condition is true. It comes after FROM. You can compare with =, <> (not equal), <, >, <= and >=. Combine conditions with AND (both must be true), OR (at least one) and NOT. Use brackets when you mix AND and OR, because AND is evaluated first.

blocks.code:
SELECT name, score
FROM students
WHERE city = 'Lahore'
  AND score > 85;
blocks.output:
name | score
------+-------
 Hira | 91   
(1 row)

blocks.html:
Only Hira is from Lahore and has a score above 85. Ayesha is from Lahore but her score is exactly 85, so score > 85 is false for her.

BETWEEN, IN, LIKE and NULL

SQL has shortcuts for common tests. BETWEEN 70 AND 80 includes both ends. IN ('CS', 'EE') checks against a list. LIKE matches text patterns: % stands for any number of characters and _ for exactly one. A missing value is NULL, and you must test it with IS NULL or IS NOT NULL, because = NULL never matches anything.

blocks.code:
SELECT name, dept, score
FROM students
WHERE score BETWEEN 70 AND 80
  AND dept IN ('SE', 'CS');

SELECT name
FROM students
WHERE name LIKE 'S%';
blocks.output:
name  | dept | score
-------+------+-------
 Bilal | SE   | 72   
 Sara  | SE   | 78   
(2 rows)

 name
------
 Sara
(1 row)

blocks.html:
Bilal (72) and Sara (78) are the SE students between 70 and 80. The pattern 'S%' means "starts with S", which matches only Sara.

Sorting and limiting

Rows come back in no guaranteed order unless you ask. ORDER BY sorts the result: ASC is ascending (the default) and DESC is descending. You can sort by several columns; the second column is used to break ties. LIMIT n keeps only the first n rows, which is perfect for "top 3" questions. (SQL Server writes SELECT TOP 3 instead.)

blocks.code:
SELECT name, score
FROM students
ORDER BY score DESC
LIMIT 3;
blocks.output:
name   | score
--------+-------
 Hira   | 91   
 Ayesha | 85   
 Sara   | 78   
(3 rows)

blocks.html:
The clauses always appear in this order: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT. Writing them in another order is a syntax error.

Common mistakes

  • Writing WHERE score = NULL. Use IS NULL.
  • Mixing AND and OR without brackets and getting surprising rows.
  • Expecting a particular order without ORDER BY.

Key Points

  • WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true.
  • Combine tests with AND, OR, NOT; use brackets to be clear.
  • BETWEEN, IN and LIKE are shortcuts for common conditions.
  • Test missing values with IS NULL, never = NULL.
  • ORDER BY sorts and LIMIT keeps the first rows.

INSERT, UPDATE & DELETE

Adding rows with INSERT

So far we only read data. INSERT INTO adds a new row. Name the columns in brackets, then give the matching values in the same order. Always name the columns: the query keeps working even if someone later adds a column to the table. A column you leave out gets its default value (usually NULL).

blocks.output:
INSERT 1 row

 id | name   | score
----+--------+-------
 6  | Zainab | 70   
(1 row)

blocks.html:
You can insert many rows in one statement by repeating the brackets after VALUES, separated by commas.

Changing rows with UPDATE

UPDATE changes existing rows. SET says which columns get which new values, and WHERE says which rows. The WHERE clause is not optional in practice: an UPDATE without WHERE changes every row in the table. Imagine setting every student's score to 75 by accident. Make it a habit to run the same condition as a SELECT first and check the rows it returns.

blocks.output:
UPDATE 1 row

 id | name  | score
----+-------+-------
 4  | Usman | 75   
(1 row)

blocks.html:
Usman's score changed from 64 to 75 and no other row was touched, because the condition matched only id = 4.

Removing rows with DELETE

DELETE FROM removes rows, and again WHERE decides which. DELETE FROM students; with no condition empties the whole table. Deleted rows are gone for good unless you have a backup or you are inside a transaction that you can ROLLBACK. In real applications many teams avoid deleting and instead add a column such as is_active, so the data can be recovered.

blocks.output:
DELETE 1 row

 students_left
---------------
 5            
(1 row)

blocks.html:
Key Points

  • INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (values); adds a row.
  • UPDATE table SET column = value WHERE condition; changes rows.
  • DELETE FROM table WHERE condition; removes rows.
  • Without WHERE, UPDATE and DELETE affect every row.
  • Test the condition with SELECT before you change data.

Combining Tables with JOIN

Why we split data into tables

A database does not keep everything in one huge table. Students, courses and the grades that connect them live in separate tables, so each fact is stored once. Besides students we now use courses and enrollments. An enrollment row says "student 1 took course 2 and got a B". The columns student_id and course_id point to rows in the other tables.

coursesenrollments
idtitlecreditsstudent_idcourse_idgrade
1Databases311A
2Web Engineering312B
3Assembly Language221B
31A
33A
52C

To see names instead of ids you must join the tables.

INNER JOIN

A JOIN glues rows from two tables together. The ON clause says how they match, usually "the id in one table equals the id stored in the other". An INNER JOIN (just JOIN for short) keeps only rows that have a match on both sides. Give tables short aliases such as s and e and write the alias before the column (s.name) so there is no confusion when two tables have a column with the same name.

blocks.code:
SELECT s.name, e.grade
FROM students s
INNER JOIN enrollments e
  ON e.student_id = s.id
WHERE e.course_id = 1;
blocks.output:
name   | grade
--------+-------
 Ayesha | A    
 Bilal  | B    
 Hira   | A    
(3 rows)

blocks.html:
Three students took Databases (course 1). Usman and Sara do not appear because they have no enrollment in course 1.

LEFT JOIN keeps everyone from the left

A LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table, even when there is no match on the right. For those rows the columns of the right table are filled with NULL. This is how you find "students with no enrollments": join, then keep the rows where the right side is NULL. RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image, and FULL JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides (not available in every database).

blocks.code:
SELECT s.name, e.course_id
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN enrollments e
  ON e.student_id = s.id
WHERE e.course_id IS NULL;
blocks.output:
name  | course_id
-------+-----------
 Usman | NULL     
(1 row)

blocks.html:
Usman (id 4) has no enrollment at all, so an INNER JOIN would have dropped him, but the LEFT JOIN kept him with NULL in the course column.

Joining three tables

You can chain joins. Here we connect students to courses through the enrollments table, which sits in the middle.

blocks.code:
SELECT s.name, c.title, e.grade
FROM students s
JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id
JOIN courses c     ON c.id = e.course_id
WHERE s.city = 'Lahore'
ORDER BY s.name, c.title;
blocks.output:
name   | title             | grade
--------+-------------------+-------
 Ayesha | Databases         | A    
 Ayesha | Web Engineering   | B    
 Hira   | Assembly Language | A    
 Hira   | Databases         | A    
(4 rows)

blocks.html:
Key Points

  • A JOIN combines rows from two tables using a matching condition in ON.
  • INNER JOIN keeps only rows that match on both sides.
  • LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the left table; missing matches become NULL.
  • Use LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL to find rows with no match.
  • Use table aliases and write alias.column to avoid confusion.

COUNT, SUM, AVG & GROUP BY

Aggregate functions

An aggregate function reads many rows and returns a single value. COUNT(*) counts rows, SUM(col) adds, AVG(col) averages, MIN(col) and MAX(col) find the smallest and largest. COUNT(col) counts only the rows where col is not NULL, while COUNT(*) counts all rows. Aggregates ignore NULL values (except COUNT(*)).

blocks.code:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS students,
       AVG(score) AS average,
       MAX(score) AS highest,
       MIN(score) AS lowest
FROM students;

blocks.html:
The whole table became one row. To find who has the highest score, you cannot put name next to MAX(score) directly; use ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 1 or a subquery (next lesson).

GROUP BY: one result per group

GROUP BY splits the rows into groups that share the same value and applies the aggregate to each group. Every column in the SELECT list must either be in the GROUP BY or be inside an aggregate function. Think of it as "for each city, give me the number of students and their average".

blocks.code:
SELECT city,
       COUNT(*) AS students,
       AVG(score) AS average
FROM students
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY students DESC, city;
blocks.output:
city      | students | average
-----------+----------+---------
 Karachi   | 2        | 75.0   
 Lahore    | 2        | 88.0   
 Islamabad | 1        | 64.0   
(3 rows)

blocks.html:
WHERE or HAVING?

WHERE filters rows before they are grouped. HAVING filters groups after the aggregates are calculated, so it is the only place where you can write a condition on COUNT, AVG and friends. A good test: if the condition needs an aggregate, it belongs in HAVING; otherwise use WHERE, which is also faster.

blocks.code:
SELECT dept, AVG(score) AS average
FROM students
WHERE score >= 70
GROUP BY dept
HAVING AVG(score) > 78
ORDER BY dept;

blocks.html:
First WHERE removed Usman (64). Then the rows were grouped by department and only CS (average 88) passed HAVING AVG(score) > 78. SE averages 75, so it was dropped.

Aggregates with joins

Joins and grouping work together. This query counts how many students took each course, including courses nobody took if you use a LEFT JOIN from courses.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.title, COUNT(e.student_id) AS taken
FROM courses c
LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.title
ORDER BY taken DESC, c.title;
blocks.output:
title             | taken
-------------------+-------
 Databases         | 3    
 Web Engineering   | 2    
 Assembly Language | 1    
(3 rows)

blocks.html:
Key Points

  • COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX turn many rows into one value.
  • GROUP BY makes one result row per group.
  • Every selected column is either grouped or inside an aggregate.
  • WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after.
  • COUNT(col) skips NULL; COUNT(*) does not.

Subqueries & Combining Results

A query inside a query

A subquery is a SELECT written inside another query, in brackets. The database runs the inner query first and uses its result in the outer one. The classic example answers "who scored above the average?". You cannot write WHERE score > AVG(score) directly, because WHERE works on single rows and cannot use an aggregate. A subquery solves it in one step.

blocks.code:
SELECT name, score
FROM students
WHERE score > (SELECT AVG(score) FROM students)
ORDER BY score DESC;
blocks.output:
name   | score
--------+-------
 Hira   | 91   
 Ayesha | 85   
(2 rows)

blocks.html:
The average score is 78. The inner query returns that single number and the outer query keeps the students above it. Sara (78) is not included because 78 is not greater than 78.

IN and NOT IN with a list of values

When the inner query returns a column of values, test against it with IN. This finds students who took at least one course, and NOT IN finds the others. Be careful: if the inner list contains a NULL, NOT IN returns nothing at all. NOT EXISTS or a LEFT JOIN is safer for that question.

blocks.output:
name  
--------
 Ayesha
 Hira  
(2 rows)

 name 
-------
 Usman
(1 row)

blocks.html:
Ayesha and Hira earned an A. In the second query the inner part refers to s.id from the outer query (a correlated subquery), so it is checked once per student. Only Usman has no enrollments.

UNION: stacking two results

UNION puts the rows of two queries one after the other. Both queries must return the same number of columns with compatible types. UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps them and is faster. It is useful when similar data lives in two tables, for example current students and alumni.

blocks.code:
SELECT name, 'top' AS band FROM students WHERE score >= 85
UNION ALL
SELECT name, 'needs help' FROM students WHERE score < 70
ORDER BY name;
blocks.output:
name   | band      
--------+------------
 Ayesha | top       
 Hira   | top       
 Usman  | needs help
(3 rows)

blocks.html:
Key Points

  • A subquery is a SELECT inside brackets, used by the outer query.
  • Use a subquery to compare with an aggregate, like score > (SELECT AVG(score) ...).
  • IN and EXISTS test against the rows of a subquery.
  • NOT IN misbehaves when the list has NULL; prefer NOT EXISTS.
  • UNION stacks results (no duplicates); UNION ALL keeps duplicates.

Keys, Constraints & Relationships

Primary keys

Every table should have a primary key: a column (or group of columns) whose value is unique and never NULL, so it identifies exactly one row. Usually it is a number that the database generates, such as id. Names make poor keys, because two students can share a name. A primary key also gets an index automatically, so searching by it is fast.

Foreign keys and relationships

A foreign key is a column that stores the primary key of a row in another table. It creates a relationship and lets the database protect it: you cannot enroll a student who does not exist, and you cannot delete a course that still has enrollments (unless you choose ON DELETE CASCADE). The most common relationship is one-to-many: one department has many students, so the students table stores the department id.

A many-to-many relationship, like students and courses (a student takes many courses and a course has many students), cannot be stored in either table directly. You add a third table, a junction table. That is exactly what enrollments is: each row links one student to one course, and each of its two columns is a foreign key.

Creating tables with constraints

Constraints are rules the database enforces for you. NOT NULL forbids missing values, UNIQUE forbids duplicates (a good fit for an email address), CHECK tests a condition and DEFAULT supplies a value when none is given. Putting rules in the database is safer than only checking in your application, because every program that touches the data must obey them.

blocks.output:
CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE

blocks.html:
The junction table uses a composite primary key made of both columns, so the same student cannot be enrolled in the same course twice.

What happens when a rule is broken?

If a query violates a constraint, the database refuses it and returns an error, and nothing is saved. For example, inserting a second user with an existing email fails because of UNIQUE, and inserting a score of 150 fails because of CHECK. Read these errors carefully: they tell you which rule you broke.

blocks.output:
INSERT 1 row

ERROR: duplicate value violates UNIQUE constraint "users.email"
(nothing was inserted)

blocks.html:
Key Points

  • A primary key is unique, never NULL and identifies one row.
  • A foreign key points to a primary key in another table and keeps the data consistent.
  • One-to-many: store the parent id in the child table.
  • Many-to-many needs a junction table with two foreign keys.
  • NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK and DEFAULT let the database enforce your rules.

Indexes, Views & Normalization

Indexes: faster reads, slower writes

Without help, finding a row by city means reading the whole table, row by row. An index is a sorted lookup structure (like the index at the back of a book) that lets the database jump straight to the matching rows. Create indexes on columns you often use in WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY. Primary keys and UNIQUE columns are indexed automatically.

The trade-off: every index takes extra disk space, and every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE must also update the index, so writes get slower. Indexing every column is a mistake. Add indexes where reads are frequent and slow, and measure the result.

blocks.output:
CREATE INDEX

 name 
-------
 Bilal
 Sara 
(2 rows)

blocks.html:
Views: saved queries

A view is a saved SELECT that you can read like a table. It stores no data itself; the query runs every time you read from it. Views keep complicated joins in one place, give each user a simpler picture of the data, and can hide sensitive columns such as passwords.

blocks.output:
CREATE VIEW

 name   | dept | score
--------+------+-------
 Hira   | CS   | 91   
 Ayesha | CS   | 85   
(2 rows)

blocks.html:
You read from the view with FROM top_students, exactly as if it were a table. If a student's score changes in students, the view shows the new result automatically.

Normalization in plain words

Normalization means organizing tables so that each fact is stored once. Bad design repeats data: if every enrollment row also stored the course title and the student's city, then renaming a course means editing many rows, and one missed row leaves the data contradicting itself. The usual steps are:

  • 1NF: each cell holds one value. No lists like "Databases, Web" in a single column.
  • 2NF: every column depends on the whole key, not just a part of it.
  • 3NF: columns depend only on the key, not on other non-key columns. A city's province belongs in a cities table, not in every student row.

Normalized designs avoid update mistakes. Sometimes people denormalize on purpose (keep a copy) to make a slow report faster, but that is a decision to make carefully, after measuring.

Key Points

  • An index speeds up reads but slows down writes and uses space.
  • Index the columns you often filter, join and sort by, not everything.
  • A view is a saved query; you read from it with FROM view_name.
  • Normalization stores each fact once: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF.
  • Denormalize only on purpose, after measuring.
